# A quadratic normal cost in an anisotropic seven-fiber depth response

This is an actual \(n=d=2\) mixed-source response theorem. The small
fibers have widths of orders \(t^{3/4}\) and \(t^{1/4}\), area of
order \(t\), and centroid \(g\). Normal motions of order \(\sqrt t\)
have both an ordinary-simplex cost and an added-fiber benefit of
order \(t\). Both terms must be retained. This differs from the
constant-length, width-\(t\) strip response and from a bounded
isotropic tangent-body limit.

## 1. Actual source and statement

Let
\[
T=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2),\quad V=\tfrac12,\quad
g=(\tfrac13,\tfrac13),\quad
\Gamma=\tfrac49,\quad \kappa=\tfrac23.
\]
Write \(l_1(v)=v_1,\ l_2(v)=v_2,\ l_0(v)=-v_1-v_2\).
Fix \(\eta=1/10\) and define
\[
B=M_\eta(T-g),\qquad
M_\eta=\begin{pmatrix}1&-\eta\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
E_t=g+\operatorname{diag}(t^{3/4},t^{1/4})B.
\tag{1}
\]
Thus \(B\) has centroid zero and area \(V\), and \(|E_t|=tV\).
Its vertices before the diagonal scaling are
\[
(-3/10,-1/3),\quad(7/10,-1/3),\quad(-2/5,2/3).
\]
For example \(0<t^{1/4}\le1/4\) makes \(E_t\subset\operatorname{int}T\):
each coordinate is positive after adding \(g\), and the sum is at
most \(2/3+(7/10)/64+(2/3)/4<1\).

Put \(T\) at the four binary bases \(Q=\{0,1\}^2\), and put \(E_t\)
at
\[
r=(-1,0),\qquad p=(-1,1),\qquad p'=(1,-1).
\]
Take the actual convex hull in \(\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2\).
Its projection is the quadrilateral
\[
-1\le z_1\le1,\qquad z_2\le1,\qquad z_1+2z_2\ge-1.
\]
Its integer points are exactly these seven bases. The three added
bases are exposed, and every continuous generator belongs to \(T\).
Consequently the actual fibers are precisely the stated ones, and
the hull is full dimensional. Its mixed mass is
\[
M_t=4V+3tV.
\tag{2}
\]

Define
\[
H(x)=x^2+\frac{2(x-\eta)^2}{1-x+\eta}.
\]
There is a unique \(x_*\in(0,\eta)\) satisfying
\[
(1-x_*)(1-x_*+\eta)^2=1,
\quad\text{equivalently}\quad
100x_*^3-320x_*^2+341x_*-21=0.
\tag{3}
\]
Set
\[
\Delta=\frac V9 H(x_*)>0,\qquad
J_0=J_2=2\Gamma V,\qquad J_1=2\Gamma V+\Delta,\qquad
\overline J=2\Gamma V+\Delta/3.
\tag{4}
\]
For sufficiently small \(t>0\), every global maximizing point has
the single integer base \(q=(0,0)\). Every maximizing selection has
\[
y_t=g+t v_*+o(t),\qquad
l_i(v_*)=\frac{J_i-\overline J}{\kappa}.
\tag{5}
\]
In the standard two continuous coordinates this is
\[
v_*=(\Delta,-\Delta/2).
\]
The true absolute and normalized maxima satisfy
\[
D_t=\Gamma V+t(V+\overline J)+o(t)
=\frac29+t\left(\frac{17}{18}+\frac\Delta3\right)+o(t),
\tag{6}
\]
\[
\frac{D_t}{M_t}
=\frac19+t\left(\frac7{18}+\frac\Delta6\right)+o(t).
\tag{7}
\]
There is no assertion of uniqueness of the continuous maximizer
at each finite \(t\). Formula (5) describes every maximizer.

## 2. Fixed-normal paired tails, with every shift retained

For a nonzero continuous normal \(u\), write
\[
P_B(u)=\min_{\sigma\in\mathbb R}
\left[
|B\cap\{u\cdot x\ge\sigma\}|+
|B\cap\{u\cdot x\ge-\sigma\}|
\right].
\tag{8}
\]
The minima are attained: shifts beyond the bounded projection
support give the saturated cost \(V\). All scalar laws are
nonatomic, so closed supporting cuts and open cuts have the
same area. The ordinary paired-centroid-tail theorem gives
\[
P_B(u)\ge2\Gamma V
\tag{9}
\]
for every \(u\). Here it also follows from the separately proved
all-point paired-depth identity for triangles.

For \(u=(1,x)\), pullback by \(M_\eta\) gives the normal
\((1,q)\) on \(T-g\), where \(q=x-\eta\).
When \(-1/5\le q\le0\), its three vertex heights on \(T\) are
\(q,0,1\). Their normalized heights are \(0,a,1\), with
\[
a=-q/(1-q)\in[0,1/6],\qquad m=(1+a)/3.
\]
For \(0<a<1\), the normalized upper tail is
\[
F_a(s)=
\begin{cases}
1&s\le0,\\
1-s^2/a&0\le s\le a,\\
(1-s)^2/(1-a)&a\le s\le1,\\
0&s\ge1.
\end{cases}
\tag{10}
\]
The complete piecewise-quadratic minimization of
\(F_a(m+\sigma)+F_a(m-\sigma)\) has only:
the zero-shift value, the saturation value one, and a possible
proper straddling minimum when \(a>1/2\).
To recall why, both-below-mode pieces are concave; both-above-mode
pieces are convex with their only stationary point at zero.
The proper straddling second derivative has sign \(2a-1\).
One-full pieces have value at least one, and one-empty proper
pieces increase toward saturation. At a vertex event the tail
and its first derivative agree, so no additional minimum is lost.

Our range has \(a\le1/6\), and the zero-shift value is
\[
2F_a(m)=2\left[\Gamma+\frac{q^2}{9(1-q)}\right]<1.
\]
Indeed its excess over \(8/9\) is at most \(2/225\).
The repeated-height case \(q=0\) follows either directly or by
area continuity. Thus, for every \(x\in[-\eta,\eta]\),
\[
P_B((1,x))
=2V\left[\Gamma+\frac{(x-\eta)^2}{9(1-x+\eta)}\right],
\tag{11}
\]
and zero opposite shift attains the minimum.

The \(Y\)-coordinate of \(B\) is the centered \(Y\)-coordinate of
\(T\). Its upper paired-tail sum, divided by \(V\), is
\[
\begin{cases}
8/9+2\sigma^2,&0\le\sigma\le1/3,\\
1+(2/3-\sigma)^2,&1/3\le\sigma\le2/3,\\
1,&\sigma\ge2/3.
\end{cases}
\tag{12}
\]
It has minimum \(8/9\) and maximum \(10/9\).
The lower paired sum is two minus this expression, and therefore
also has minimum \(8/9\). In particular
\[
P_B((0,1))=P_B((0,-1))=2\Gamma V.
\tag{13}
\]
The negative-\(Y\) minimum is attained at the nonzero shift \(1/3\);
it must not be replaced by its zero-shift value \(10V/9\).

## 3. Exact finite-tilt reduction and point localization

Delete the owned fiber \(R_t=E_t\) at \(r\), obtaining the six-base
source. For points \((q,y)\), the exact finite-tilt lemma in
candidate 1ec867c146e96dba gives
\[
A_{6,t}((q,y))
=\min_{|u|=1}\{F_T(y,u)+t\,P_t(u,y)\},
\tag{14}
\]
where \(P_t\) is the opposite-pair cost divided by \(t\).
Each opposite pair shift is realized by a single ambient halfspace,
with base coefficients \(\beta_1=-K+s/2,\ \beta_2=-K-s/2\).
A fixed sufficiently large \(K\) excludes the other core fibers
and captures every point of \(R_t\); a bounded shift range suffices
because \(E_t\subset T\). Vertical caps are included in the exact
lemma and cannot be minimizing near \(g\).

The canonical upper caps have pair cost at most \(tV\), by
saturating the shift, while depth at \(g\) is at least \(\Gamma V\).
Hence every local maximizer has all three barycentric coordinates
at most \(1/3+O(t)\); their sum is one, so
\[
y_t=g+O(t).
\tag{15}
\]
This localization holds for every maximizing selection and uses
only the added volume, not a limiting shape.

Section 1 of candidate 501dba519aa398a9
proves, without any weak-limit assumptions, that in a fixed
neighborhood of \(g\) and for small \(t\),
\[
A_{7,t}((q,y))=tV+A_{6,t}((q,y)).
\tag{16}
\]
The reason is the fixed positive reflected-profile gap of the
own simplex and the opposite core partner whenever \(R_t\) is
not fully captured. The bounded-tilt realization in (14) attains
the competing smaller cost while capturing all of \(R_t\).
Both local maximizing sets are in this neighborhood by (15).

## 4. All normal rates and the effective normal cost

For every convergent bounded sequence \(v_t\to v\), the exact
local first-order response is
\[
A_{6,t}((q,g+t v_t))
=\Gamma V+t\min_i\{J_i-\kappa l_i(v)\}+o(t).
\tag{17}
\]
We prove all normal regimes, including rates faster and slower
than \(\sqrt t\).

An approximately minimizing normal must approach one of the
three canonical directions: the ordinary cap at \(g\) has a
strict positive gap away from those directions, whereas the
added cost is nonnegative and canonical trial caps give an
upper bound \(\Gamma V+O(t)\).

Near the canonical \(l_1\) direction, positively rescale the
normal to \((1,\delta)\), with \(\delta\to0\).
The own cap has only the vertex \(e_1\) positive and satisfies
the exact formula
\[
F_T(g,(1,\delta))
=V\frac{(2-\delta)^2}{9(1-\delta)}
=\Gamma V+\frac{V\delta^2}{9(1-\delta)}.
\tag{18}
\]
At the moving point its exact formula is
\[
F_T(g+t v_t,(1,\delta))
=\frac V{1-\delta}
\left[\frac{2-\delta}{3}
-t(v_{t,1}+\delta v_{t,2})\right]^2.
\tag{19}
\]
Thus its point variation is \(-t\kappa v_1+o(t)\), uniformly
as \(\delta\to0\). If \(|\delta|/\sqrt t\to\infty\), (18)
divided by \(t\) diverges, while (19) changes by only \(O(t)\).
Nonnegativity of the added term rules out such an approximately
minimizing sequence. A bounded first-order cap cost therefore
forces \(\delta=\sqrt t\,x_t\) with \(x_t\) bounded.

After passing to \(x_t\to x\), the projection on the small body is
\[
(1,\delta)\cdot(X-g)
=t^{3/4}(b_1+x_t b_2),\qquad b\in B.
\]
The center threshold divided by \(t^{3/4}\) is
\[
t^{1/4}(v_{t,1}+\delta v_{t,2})\longrightarrow0.
\tag{20}
\]
For \(x_t\) in a bounded interval, \(B\) has a uniformly bounded
projection range. Saturation restricts the rescaled pair shift
to one compact interval. Cap areas then converge uniformly over
that interval: any convergent normal/shift subsequence has
indicators converging off one line, which is area-null.
Consequently the paired cost converges to \(P_B((1,x))\).
Together with (18)-(20), the limiting \(l_1\) score is
\[
-\kappa v_1+
\min_{x\in\mathbb R}
\left\{\frac{Vx^2}{9}+P_B((1,x))\right\}.
\tag{21}
\]
Every fixed \(x\) is also an admissible trial normal, so this is
an equality, not merely a lower bound.

The competitor \(x=\eta\) has cost \(2\Gamma V+V\eta^2/9\).
The universal lower bound (9) excludes \(|x|>\eta\) from
minimization. Formula (11) therefore evaluates the entire minimum:
it is \(2\Gamma V+(V/9)\min_{[-\eta,\eta]}H(x)\).
On this interval
\[
H'(x)=2\left[x+(1-x+\eta)^{-2}-1\right],\qquad
H''(x)=2+4(1-x+\eta)^{-3}>0.
\]
Its derivative is negative at zero and positive at \(\eta\).
Its unique minimizer is exactly (3), proving the stated \(J_1\).
This also justifies the compact normal-parameter restriction
without presupposing where the optimum lies.

Near \(l_2\) or \(l_0\), the \(Y\)-coefficient of the normal
stays respectively positive or negative and bounded away from
zero. Dividing the small-body projection by \(t^{1/4}\) gives
the normal \((\sqrt t\,u_1,u_2)\) on \(B\), tending to a
positive multiple of \(Y\) or of \(-Y\).
The moving-center threshold on that scale is \(O(t^{3/4})\).
The same compact-shift/area-null argument gives the pair cost
\(2\Gamma V\), at every rate of normal convergence.
The own-cap excess at \(g\) is nonnegative and its point
variation is \(-t\kappa l_i(v)+o(t)\). Exact canonical trial
normals attain those scores. No lower bound discards a negative
own-normal cost.

These arguments prove the lower half of (17) along any supposedly
violating sequence of approximately minimizing normals.
The \(l_1\) trial \(\delta=\sqrt t\,x_*\) and the two exact
canonical trials prove the matching upper bound. All closed
boundary cases are covered by the area-null convergence above.
In particular, at points \(g+t v_*+o(t)\), every cap sequence
within \(o(t)\) of the minimum whose normal approaches \(l_1\)
must satisfy \(\delta/\sqrt t\to x_*\). Boundedness follows
from (18), and every other cluster point has strictly larger
cost by the uniqueness of the minimum in (21).

## 5. Attained global optimization and exact algebraic certificate

The elementary zero-sum balance is
\[
\max_{\sum_i v_i=0}\min_i(J_i-\kappa v_i)=\overline J,
\]
with the unique optimizer \(v_i=(J_i-\overline J)/\kappa\).
Use \(g+t v_*\in T\) as a trial point. Equation (15) bounds the
rescaled displacements of every maximizing sequence. Applying
(17) to every convergent subsequence proves both the attained
local maximum \(\Gamma V+t\overline J+o(t)\) and (5).

The exact global seven-base identity from the same response note is
\[
D_t=\Gamma V+\max\{tV,tV,tV+D_{6,t}^{q}-\Gamma V\}.
\tag{22}
\]
The other core anchors have exact local maxima \(\Gamma V+tV\),
the last core anchor has maximum \(\Gamma V\), and exposed
added-base candidates have depth at most \(tV\). Their original
isolating caps remain valid for every shape \(E_t\subset T\).
Since \(\overline J>0\), the third term wins strictly for small
\(t\); all global maximizing points have base \(q\).
Equations (2), (16), and (22) prove (6)-(7), including the
normalization by all seven actual fiber masses.

For a rational isolation of the algebraic constant, the cubic
in (3) is negative at \(6553/100000\) and positive at
\(3277/50000\); strict convexity above makes the selected root
unique in this interval. Numerically, only as a calibration,
\[
x_*\simeq0.06553089269734,\qquad
\Delta\simeq0.000366186609424.
\]
The source's prescribed core centroids are strictly suboptimal:
at \((q,g)\) the coefficient is \(V+2\Gamma V=17/18\),
whereas the optimal coefficient is \(17/18+\Delta/3\).
The other core centroid coefficients are smaller still.
The normalized maximum remains strictly above the OC target
\(\Gamma/4=1/9\); this is not an OC counterexample.

The verifier uses rational \(t=\tau^4\), exact polygon clipping,
complete quadratic shift minimization for (10), and rational
isolation of (3). The compactness and all-normal limit, rather
than finite cap samples, establish the theorem.
